def: abstinent or austere in lifestyle (adj); a person who leads an austere and simple life without material pleasures, esp. someone who does this for religious reasons

def: Reach the highest point or final stage

def: Burdensome, oppressive, hard to endure

def: Ordinary, dull, commonplace

def: Judge, umpire, person empowered to decide matters at hand

def: Incapable of feeling; unconscious, unaware
example: Very intoxicated people can be insensible to pain, leading to serious problems as they injure themselves and don’t realize it.

def: Hint, suggest slyly; introduce (an idea) into someone’s mind in a subtle, artful way
example: “Where’s your boyfriend? You didn’t leave him home alone, did you?” asked Ming. “Are you insinuating something?” asked Helen. “If you have something to say, just say it.”

def: Dull, stale, lacking taste or interest
example: This is a university level poetry class, and your insipid drivel just won’t cut it here. “Things that are bad always make me sad”? Really?

def: Pertaining to an island; detached, standing alone; narrow-minded, provincial
example: The young actress couldn’t wait to escape the insularity of her small town, where life revolved around high school football and Taco Bell was considered exotic international cuisine.

def: Rebellion or revolt against a government or similarly established authority
example: Due to frequent insurrections, the nation has had six governments in just five years.

def: Bury (a dead body) or place in a tomb
example: After the funeral, the body will be interred in the cemetery.

def: Interaction, reciprocal relationship or influence
example: Bilingual readers will enjoy the interplay of English and Spanish in many of the poems in this anthology of the work of Mexican-American poets.

def: A time in between two reigns or regimes during which there is no ruler; a period during which government does not function; any period of freedom from authority or break or interruption in a series
example: When the king died with no heir, his ministers ruled in the interregnum as the nobles argued over which of the king’s nephews should rule next.

def: Refusing to compromise, inflexible, having extreme attitudes
example: “Even three detentions and a note home to your parents haven’t convinced you to behave yourself in class!” the teacher said to the intransigent child.

def: Flood, cover with water, overwhelm
example: As the city was inundated with water, the mayor feared that many evacuees would have nowhere to go.

def: Toughen up; accustom or habituate to pain, hardship, etc.
example: Having had over a dozen surgeries before she was ten, spending months at a time in the hospital, she considered herself inured to pain and disappointment.

def: Violent denunciation; accusations, insults, or verbal abuse
example: Although the money was good, she quit her job after nearly having a nervous breakdown from her boss’s invective.

def: Entice, lure; get something by flattery, cleverness, or offering incentives
example: After Mrs. Kim found out that her son’s friends had inveigled him into doing something stupid, she gave him a lecture on standing up to peer pressure.

def: Investing; formally giving someone a right or title
example: The former dean had her academic robes dry cleaned in preparation for her investiture as university president.

def: Hateful, offensive, injurious
example: School bullying has become a serious problem, with ongoing invidious behavior driving students to suicide.

def: Irritable, easily angered
example: “I spent my entire childhood tiptoeing around so as not to anger my irascible mother,” Joe told his therapist.

def: Wavering, not sure how to proceed, not firm in one’s decision-making
example: If we were voting on the bill this moment, we’d have enough votes to pass it. But many of our supporters are irresolute—we’re worried that when lobbyists get to them, they’ll quickly change their minds.

def: Traveling from place to place, esp. as part of a job
example: In rural areas in the 1940s, it was common that a small town would lack its own doctor, instead being seen by an itinerant family physician who made rounds to many such towns.

def: Travel schedule; detailed plan for a journey
example: Great, that was the Parthenon! What’s next on our itinerary?

def: Discard, cast off; throw items overboard in order to lighten a ship in an emergency
example: We got so tired while hiking the Appalachian Trail that we jettisoned some of our fancy camping supplies just so we could drag ourselves to a place where we could get medical attention.

def: Excessive, loud patriotism and aggressive, warlike foreign policy
example: He is such a jingoist that he’s always yelling at the TV, calling even the most conservative commentators “wimps” for failing to suggest that we simply nuke, burn, pillage, and otherwise extirpate our so-called “enemies.”

def: Place side-by-side (either physically or in a metaphorical way, such as to make a comparison)
example: Making a decision between two engagement rings from two different stores was difficult, he noted—it would be much easier if he could juxtapose them and compare them directly.

def: Ignite, cause to begin burning; incite, arouse, inflame
example: It’s hard to kindle a campfire when it’s so damp out.

def: Pertaining to motion
example: Marisa told her mother what she had learned in science class: a ball sitting on a table has potential energy, but a ball falling towards the ground has kinetic energy.

def: The sound made by a bell for a funeral, or any sad sound or signal of a failure, death, ending, etc. (noun); to make such a sound (verb)
example: The Senate minority leader’s speech was a death knell for the bill; all hope of bipartisan cooperation was lost.

def: Tearful, mournful
example: Accustomed to lachrymose occasions, the funeral home kept boxes of tissues near every seat.

def: Theft
example: The department store employs a security officer whose job it is to prevent larceny.

def: Generosity, the giving of money or gifts (esp. with the implication that the giver is a bit superior to the recipient)
example: While I did attend a tony private school, my parents were actually quite poor—I was at that school through the largesse of my grandfather.

def: Potential; existing but not visible or active
example: Certain experts believe that some people have a genetic propensity for addiction; however, if such a person never comes into contact with drugs, the propensity for addiction can remain latent for life.

def: Worthy of praise
example: When a major discount mart fired several employees for subduing a gunman, most people considered the action a laudable act of heroism, but the discount chain fired the employees for “violating company policies.” Nevertheless, the mayor lauded the former employees in a medal- granting ceremony.

def: Not strict; careless, loose, slack
example: My parents were really lax about homework—they never checked to see if I did it or not. Sadly, this legacy of laxity is not serving me well while studying for the GRE.

def: Suspicious or wary
example: You should be leery of any business opportunity that requires a startup fee and a “sponsor”— you might find yourself sucked into a scam.

def: Slight-of-hand (magic as performed by a magician); trickery or deception
example: The child was astounded when her uncle pulled out a quarter from behind her ear. Of course, she hadn’t actually lost a quarter there; it was just a bit of legerdemain from an amateur magician.

def: Lazy, drowsy, or sluggish
example: I do love the Golden Corral’s reasonably priced buffet, but I feel so lethargic after I eat my weight in mac-and-cheese and hand-carved turkey.

def: Sexually unrestrained; immoral; ignoring the rules
example: The licentious behavior Joe was accustomed to practicing at the local strip club was enough to get him thrown out of a nice restaurant and fired from his new job.

def: Clear, transparent; completely calm
example: Hawaii was amazing! The water was crystal clear—so limpid that when you were scuba diving, you could see ahead for what seemed like miles!

def: Treat like a celebrity
example: Being a chef has long been a prestigious profession, but it is only in the last decade or so that “celebrity chefs” have been lionized and given their own television shows.

def: Flexible, supple, agile
example: The actress exercised and stretched every day, but was ultimately told by the casting director that she wasn’t lissome enough to play a ballet dancer. The actress had to agree—“I walk like an ogre,” she said.

def: Spiritless, lacking interest or energy
example: “I’m bored, Mom,” said the listless child. “Can I have a cookie? Can we go to the park? Let’s play a game. There’s nothing to do!”

def: Furiously angry, enraged
example: Diane was livid when she discovered that her daughter had borrowed her wedding dress to wear to an ‘80s party. “I have never been angrier in my life,” she said.

def: Mournful, gloomy (sometimes in an exaggerated way)
example: Helen was having a good time at the Irish pub until the Traditional Music Hour started, and the lugubrious tunes made her cry into her Guinness.

def: Walk in a heavy or clumsy way, sometimes due to being weighed down
example: Alicia was a model and was accustomed to walking everywhere as though on a catwalk, so she was quite displeased when she broke her leg and had to lumber around in a cast, thumping the ground everywhere she went.

def: Shining, radiant, well-lit; brilliant or enlightening
example: Use our new light-reflecting shimmer blush for a luminous complexion!

def: Gruesome or excessively vivid; sensational, shocking, unrestrained
example: I do like to keep up with what celebrities are doing, but that tabloid is just too lurid for me— just look at the cover: “Worst Cellulite in Hollywood” and “Exclusive Crash Photos.” Truly horrible.

def: Crafty schemes or plots
example: It’s cute to think that teen idols became famous because their talent was simply so great that the music industry reached out to them, but usually, any teen idol is the product of intense coaching and parental machinations.

def: Violent whirlpool; any chaotic, turbulent situation
example: The Smiths lost their houseboat in a maelstrom, but were at least thankful that they weren’t on the boat at the time and thus escaped the violent storm at sea.

def: High-minded, noble, lofty; generous in forgiving others, free of resentment
example: The twins were so different from one another—while Andrea was petty and vengeful and would hold a grudge for years, Marina was quite magnanimous, easily forgiving insults or slights, and simply rising above the petty bickering and cliquish behavior of our high school.

def: Very important or influential person, esp. in business
example: Many students pursue MBAs in hopes of becoming wealthy and powerful magnates; some students never quite make it there, instead spending their careers staring at spreadsheets and taking orders from magnates.

def: A curse
example: Sheila thought the fortune-teller was her friend, but when she didn’t pay her bill, the fortune teller cast a hex on her, a malediction intended to cause terrible things to befall her.

def: Pretend to be sick, esp. to get out of work, duties, etc.
example: Joey was sick in class on Monday and was sent to the school nurse to sleep it off. The next day, having realized that illness was a good way to get out of class, Joey said his stomach hurt and spent the afternoon in the nurse’s office. By Wednesday, though, the nurse accused him of malingering and sent him back to class.

def: Obvious, apparent, perceptible to the eye (adj); to show, make clear, or prove (verb)
example: My superstitious aunt claims that she saw a manifestation of our deceased grandfather, who appeared during a thunderstorm to warn us all about our cousin’s fiance.

def: Having a particular manner, esp. an artificial one
example: Although he grew up in rural Ohio, sometime before he got his own makeover show on television he adopted a mannered way of speaking, as though he had grown up in some very odd corner of Victorian England.

def: Damage, spoil, ruin
example: The interior designer’s secret was to buy furnishings and fixtures that had been marred on the shop floor and therefore were sold at steep discounts; she would then fix the defects herself or add additional aging effects to the pieces.

def: Person who adheres to rules extremely closely; strict disciplinarian
example: It was no fun growing up with a military officer for a dad. He was such a martinet he once made me do twenty pushups for being one minute late to bed—even though the reason I was late was that I wanted to kiss him goodnight.

def: Excessively sentimental, showing sadness or some other emotion in a foolish or silly way
example: I had no idea the film was going to be a maudlin affair in which the male lead dies and the female lead has his baby, who then also dies. Half the theater was weeping, and the other half was just shaking their heads at how badly written the movie was.

def: A general truth or fundamental principle, esp. expressed as a proverb or saying
example: My favorite maxim is “Seize the day!” How much would it cost to get that on a tattoo? How much more for “Curiosity killed the cat”?

def: Beggar, or religious follower who lives by begging
example: Having joined a mendicant order, the friar had vowed not to own property, and instead to subsist on the donations of the faithful.

def: Attractive in a vulgar or flashy way, tawdry; deceptive
example: The singer performed her concert draped in what looked from far away like precious jewels. Up close, though, the fan could see that the accessories were just meretricious plastic, glittery junk, like what little girls buy at the mall.

def: Concerned with abstract thought, related to metaphysics (branch of philosophy concerned with explaining the nature of being and of the world); very subtle or abstruse
example: My poetry class has all kinds. In contrast to Gary’s poetry about dogs and horses, Neil’s poetry is very metaphysical, exploring the relation of mortal humans to a timeless universe. It’s a little over Gary’s head.

def: Environment, atmosphere; the environmental setting in which something happens or develops
example: Becoming a priest in the anything-goes milieu of the 1960s gave Father Bryant an interesting perspective on two contrasting philosophies.

def: Have a great effect, weigh heavily (often as militate against)
example: While his resume was stellar, his speech impediment militated against his performance in job interviews.

def: Stuck, entangled (in something, like a swamp or muddy area), soiled
example: Mired in her predecessor’s mess and mistakes, the new CEO found it difficult to take the company in a new direction.

def: Jollity, merriment; amusement or laughter
example: Nothing could beat the mirth of the office holiday party—once everyone had heard how fat their bonuses would be, the delighted staff formed a conga line and drank and danced the night away.

def: Hater of humankind
example: He is such a misanthrope that when some Girl Scouts going door-to-door asked if he’d like to sponsor a hungry child overseas, he replied, “The fewer people in the world, the better,” and shut the door in their faces!

def: Letter, written message
example: While Don was overseas fighting in World War II, he lived for the missives from the wife he had left behind.

def: A little bit or limited quantity
example: In her first five years in Hollywood, she experienced only a modicum of success as an actress, appearing twice in commercials and once as a waitress on Desperate Housewives.

def: Stylish, contemporary
example: While some sculptors sought to make their work universal and timeless, Dania sculpted modish creations that captured the pop cultural zeitgeist—for instance, a sculpture of Rihanna with an umbrella, or a three-foot high representation of the latest Alexander McQueen heels.

def: Shed or cast off, esp. to regularly shed skin, feathers, etc. (as a snake)
example: Wow, the special effects in that movie were really cool! The actress grew scales all over her body and then molted, leaving behind a scaly skin covering shaped like an entire woman, and then she looked like herself again.

def: Relating to or resembling a monastery (where monks or nuns live), esp. by being quiet, secluded, contemplative, strict, and/or lacking luxuries
example: Christine decided that the only way she was going to finish her Ph.D. was to live a monastic lifestyle: she broke up with her boyfriend, cancelled her cable service, left the house only when necessary, and ultimately had a draft of her dissertation a few months later.

def: Gloomy, sullen
example: She had always been a happy child, but once she hit high school and decided to become a goth, she adopted a morose attitude to match her all-black clothing.

def: Diverse, having a lot of variety
example: Last year’s jewelry line was all metal and neutrals, but this year’s presents a multifarious array of brilliant colors.

def: Generous, giving liberally
example: The elderly titan of industry was notoriously miserly, sometimes called “the cheapest man alive.” But his wife was quite munificent, and after his death, she used his fortune to support numerous charities and to buy a house for their longtime maid.

def: Near-sighted; lacking long-term thinking, short-sighted
example: To raise prices in a time of crisis is both wrong and deeply myopic—our profits would go up in the short term, but our customers’ resentment would simmer for decades.

def: Lowest point
example: It was only when Ming reached her absolute nadir—what her recovery program called “rock bottom”—that she admitted she had a problem and checked herself into rehab.

def: New word or phrase (or a new meaning applied to an existing word or phrase)
example: You won’t find “fauxhawk” in the dictionary—it’s a neologism that describes a fake mohawk (faux means fake and is pronounced “foe”) created by sculpting the hair into a mohawk-like crest without actually shaving the sides.

def: Beginner, novice; person newly converted to a religion
example: It was totally outrageous of our law firm to send a neophyte into the courtroom to defend our case against a team of experienced attorneys.

def: Irritate, sting, or annoy
example: His first year in college, my little brother failed gym. How is that even possible? I always remind him about it just to nettle him. Of course, he usually strikes back by reminding me of that time I crashed an amusement park’s go-cart.

def: Offensive, disgusting; harmful
example: Everyone knows that smoking is deadly, but even “herbal” cigarettes are a noisome habit— and noisome to your health!

def: Trivial, so small as to be unimportant; in name only, so-called
example: A notary public will certify a document for a nominal fee, usually under $3.

def: Important or big enough to matter
example: The chief of staff told the assembled doctors, “We all make mistakes. But this mistake was nontrivial, and there is going to be an investigation.”

def: Implying or attempting to establish a norm; expressing value judgments or telling people what to do (rather than merely describing that which is happening)
example: The reason we are not understanding each other in this argument about grammar is that you are arguing normatively, telling me how people should talk, and I am simply reporting and analyzing how people actually talk.

def: Stubborn, hardhearted, hardened in wrongdoing
example: The first mate reported that there was some fuzzy shape on the horizon, but the captain insisted that the instruments showed no such object, and obdurately sailed straight ahead—right into an iceberg.

def: Slanting or sloping; indirect, misleading, or evasive
example: After the fifteenth oblique reference that Bella made to George or George made to Bella, everyone in the office figured out that they were dating.

def: Stop up, close, shut in or shut off
example: This drain guard is here to make sure nothing (like silverware) ends up occluding your garbage disposal.

def: Express an opinion
example: After all was said and done, he opined that he wished he had never tried to sail around the world in a canoe, and he was sorry that the rescue effort was so expensive.

def: Disgrace and disapproval that result from outrageously shameful actions
example: Some young starlets seem to think a DUI offense isn’t such a big deal, but drunk driving deserves opprobrium—driving under the influence maims and kills innocent people every year.

def: Full, rich, and clear (of the voice or speaking); pompous, bombastic
example: The actor James Earl Jones has long been sought after for voiceover work as well as acting jobs because of his dignified, orotund voice.

def: Become bone or become hard like bone; become inflexible in attitudes, opinions, etc.
example: I remember having many broad-ranging discussions with him back in college, but since then, his opinions have ossified—sadly, he is now the most close-minded person I know.

def: Professed, evident, or pretended; outwardly appearing in a certain way
example: Ostensibly, she came to volunteer out of the goodness of her heart. However, I think she’s really here because she has a crush on one of the other volunteers.

def: Pretentious, boastful showiness
example: Her ostentatious clothing is simply not appropriate in a business environment—in fact, nothing emblazoned with 2,000 Swarovski crystals is.

def: Overly nervous, agitated, or excited; too ornate, elaborate, or fussy; overdone
example: By the time her boyfriend met her in the park, she was overwrought, thinking he must have chosen a public place so he could break up with her—turned out, he had just invited her to a picnic.

def: Suitable for or resembling a palace, magnificent
example: After a career spent in budget hotels, she was thrilled when the client put her up in a palatial room at a five-star hotel. She raided the minibar and then promptly fell asleep on the 600-thread- count duvet.

def: Make less serious or severe; relieve symptoms of an illness
example: The doctors said it would be pointless to subject Uncle Al to continued treatments when there was no hope of a cure, so we gave consent for him to be transferred to the palliative care wing where he would be made as comfortable as possible in his final weeks or months.

def: Abnormally pale (as skin); lacking color or vitality
example: When Eric left the office mid-day, we knew from the pallor that had overtaken him that he really was getting sick.

def: Flair, style, swagger; a flamboyant or grand way of acting
example: Not only did he quit, but he did so with panache, actually delivering a Powerpoint presentation that we thought would be about the budget, but which turned out to be quite obscene. He then pulled out a flask, guzzled its contents, and walked out. That guy’s kind of a legend.

def: Formal or lofty expression of praise
example: Lincoln enthusiasts were excited that a new biography was to be published, and many hoped that new light would be cast on certain controversies. However, the book was pure panegyric— nothing but heroic tales, uncritically presented.

def: Splendid, wide-ranging, impressive display or array
example: Our old cafeteria had only premade salads, but the new cafeteria has a salad bar with a panoply of toppings.

def: Model of excellence, perfect example
example: Unlike his sister, he was a paragon of responsibility, taking in her three children when she went to jail, and even switching jobs so he could be there to pick them up from school.

def: Peel or cut off the outer layer (such as peeling fruit with a knife), reduce or trim as if cutting off the outer parts
example: We need to pare down our budget if we’re going to survive on unemployment for awhile.

def: Discussion, negotiation, esp. between enemies (noun); to have such a discussion (verb)
example: The industry trade show is our chance to parley with our competitors. We do go out for drinks together, but really, we’re just hoping someone slips up and tells us about their new product line.

def: Deflect or avoid (esp. a blow or attack); skillfully evade (a question)
example: When asked by a reporter if rumors of his infidelity were true, the candidate parried, answering that he had always supported legislation bolstering the sanctity of marriage.

def: Mix of incongruous parts; artistic work imitating the work of other artists, often satirically
example: The slickly-produced boy band’s first album was deeply unimaginative, just a pastiche of every other boy band album ever produced.

def: Capable of producing disease
example: Many common and legal food additives are pathogenic, known to lead to diabetes or even cancer.

def: Person who pays excessive attention to book learning and rules, or who uses his or her learning to show off
example: I hate when pedants interrupt you to correct your grammar, especially if what you’re saying is important—and in my opinion, almost anything is more important than pedantic quibbles over whether it’s okay to end a sentence with a preposition.

def: Travel around while selling; sell illegally; give out or disseminate
example: After an unsuccessful year spent peddling cutlery door-to-door, he turned to peddling drugs, thus landing himself in jail.

def: Disparaging, derogatory, belittling (adj); a name or word that is disparaging (noun)
example: I’m open to constructive criticism, but I think my supervisor’s remarks are inappropriately pejorative—it’s never okay to call an employee a “sniveling dullard.”

def: Transparent, translucent; clear, easy to understand
example: He decided that the cove’s pellucid waters were an excellent place to teach his daughter to swim, reasoning that, if she started to sink, he would easily be able to see where she was.

def: Regretful, feeling remorse for one’s sins or misdeeds (adj); a person who feels this way (noun)
example: After being “separated” from the college for plagiarism, she wrote a letter to the Dean expressing her deep regret and penitence and hoping to be readmitted.

def: Outer part of a shadow from an eclipse; any surrounding region, fringe, periphery; any area where something “sort of” exists
example: The Constitution doesn’t specifically mention a right to privacy, but some experts consider this to exist in the penumbra of the Constitution, as a guarantee of privacy is needed in order to exercise the rights that are enumerated.

def: Extreme poverty or scarcity
example: The young model married an elderly billionaire thinking she’d be set for life, but she ended up living in penury after her husband died and his middle-aged children held up the probate case for years, keeping her from receiving any money whatsoever.

def: Intrinsically; by itself; in itself
example: The policy isn’t sexist, per se, but it has had a disproportionate impact on women that deserves further study.

def: Travel from place to place, esp. on foot
example: After college, he took a year off to peregrinate across the country, visiting friends and seeing the forty-odd states he had never before had the chance to see.

def: Lasting through the years or indefinitely, enduring; recurring
example: Fighting over the bathroom is a perennial problem in our house—there are eight of us, and we’re homeschooled, so we’re all pretty much always here.

def: Done superficially, without much care, or merely as routine
example: She did a really perfunctory job on this Powerpoint. Sure, it has a dozen slides, but most of them just say things like “Sales—Ways to Improve” in Times New Roman on a white background. Maybe she’s planning to fill in the details later.

def: Journeying from place to place; traveling on foot
example: He quit his office job to become a peripatetic musician, traveling from town to town playing in bars and sleeping on couches.

def: Very harmful or destructive, deadly
example: Bullying has a pernicious effect on the learning environment, keeping victims too intimidated to speak up and also silencing others who fear that they could be next.

def: Having penetrating insight or good discernment
example: A good detective is shrewd and perspicacious, judging when someone is lying, noticing things the rest of us would ignore, and making connections that allow an investigation to move forward.

def: Formation of soldiers carrying shields close together for defense; any very close group of people
example: To even enter the embassy, the diplomats had to make their way through a phalanx of protestors.

def: Person deficient in or hostile to culture
example: Her date was very handsome, but she decided he was an absolute philistine when he said that documentaries were “boring” and that the “Best Picture” Oscar should go to Resident Evil: Afterlife 3D.

def: Apathetic, sluggish, not easily excited or made emotional
example: A phlegmatic child, he declined to participate in the youth soccer league. He preferred to stay at home, mostly sitting outside poking at dirt with a stick, and occasionally stopping for naptime.

def: A shallow, overused statement; cliche
example: Everyone who knew my mother knows she was an atheist, so I can’t imagine why people at her funeral would think we’d enjoy their soppy platitudes about Mom’s “being in a better place now.”

def: Of the common people
example: I toured a luxury apartment building and I laughed when I saw that the apartments had luxurious walk-in closets and whirlpool bathtubs—but hilariously tiny ovens. Because, of course, the wealthy would never do something so plebian as cook their own food.

def: Excess; excessive amount
example: She had a plethora of excuses, but there is simply no justification for arriving to class drunk.

def: Brave, spirited
example: Feminist critics have commented that today’s romantic comedies tend to feature passive, helpless female leads, whereas the romantic comedies of the 1940s featured plucky heroines who took the lead in cleverly solving problems.

def: Rule by the wealthy
example: There have always been rich and poor people, of course, but some argue that the U.S. is becoming a plutocracy, with the richest 10% controlling two-thirds of the nation’s wealth and nearly half of our Congressional representatives being millionaires.

def: Controversial argument, esp. one attacking a specific idea
example: Laura Kipnis’ 2003 book Against Love: A Polemic has been called “shocking” and “scathing.” Perhaps Kipnis used the word polemic in the title to indicate that she’s making an extreme argument as a means of starting a debate. After all, who’s really against love?

def: Shrewd, pragmatic; tactful or diplomatic
example: Celebrities have to watch what they say, as even an offhand comment can end up splashed across the covers of magazines. When the starlet was asked what she thought of her ex-husband marrying the swimsuit model he left her for, she gave the politic reply, “I wish both of them the best.”

def: Speaking or composed of many languages (of a person, book, etc.); a person who knows several languages
example: New York’s public service announcements often take the form of polyglot posters in the subway, suggesting in six languages that readers give up their seats for pregnant women or those with disabilities.

def: Presume, suggest, put forward (an idea)
example: For thousands of years, philosophers have thought of the self as a unified entity, but neuroscientists today posit the existence of a modular brain—a self that is a mix of different brain parts, with no central “coordinator.”

def: Talk in an idle, simple-minded, meaningless, or foolish way; chatter, babble
example: It was infuriating to listen to the boss prattle on about some new restaurant in town when everyone was just waiting to find out if they’d been laid off.

def: Cause to happen suddenly or prematurely; fling, plunge, or hurl down
example: Mr. and Mrs. Rosen had been considering a move to Florida for years, but the sudden destruction of their house in a hurricane precipitated their decision to finally make the move.

def: Concise summary, abstract
example: Just as scientific journals publish abstracts of their articles online (and then charge for access to the full version), the entrepreneur decided to publish a précis of her whitepaper online, while charging for access to the full version.

def: Preference, tendency or favorability towards
example: She has completed teacher training allowing her to teach grades K–6, but she discovered that she really has a predilection for teaching kindergarten.

def: Having foreknowledge or foresight, seeing the future
example: Mariposa swears she’s prescient—she thinks she sees the future in her dreams.

def: Supernatural, exceptional
example: While Tiger Woods has been mired in scandal, his preternatural golfing talent is still undeniable.

def: Stray from the truth, mislead, lie
example: Maryanne had been shoplifting—when her mother asked where her new clothes had come from, she prevaricated, vaguely suggesting that a rich friend had bought them for her.

def: The state of being first or most important
example: The conservative Senator argued that the very fabric of society depended on the primacy of the family, and that legislation was needed to shore up the institution of marriage.

def: Inclination, natural tendency
example: After his therapist pointed out that he had a natural proclivity to judge people prematurely, he tried to work on that by imagining things from the other person’s point of view.

def: Excessively long and wordy (of a person, piece of writing, etc.)
example: My mother is incredibly verbose. She’ll tell a boring, prolix story for five whole minutes, and at the end, it turns out that the point was that she got a fifty cent discount on a box of spaghetti at the store.

def: Reproduce, spread, increase
example: Hackers can take down a large computer system in days or even minutes as a virus propagates and infects all of the machines on a network.

def: Natural inclination or tendency
example: He was an introvert with a propensity for solitary brooding, and thus was considered a bit strange or unfriendly by the others in his dorm.

def: Relating to prophesy, predicting, ominous
example: While most of the country was consumed with irrational optimism about the economy, this particular journalist possessed an almost prophetic pessimism—not only did she predict the crash, she even predicted the month it actually happened.

example: The ancient Greeks would often attempt to propitiate angry gods by sacrificing animals to them.

def: Favorable, giving good signs for the future, likely to work out; kind or forgiving
example: After having to postpone the game earlier in the week due to rain, the officials were pleased to see the propitious weather forecast. “We’ll get this game in after all,” one of them exclaimed.

def: Agent, substitute, person authorized to act on behalf of another
example: She was in the hospital, but certainly didn’t want to miss voting on the proposal, so she sent a proxy to the board meeting to vote “yes.”

def: Juvenile, immature

def: boxing, fighting with the fists

def: Power, might
example: When people asked the twenty-five year old bride what had attracted her to her commanding, sixty year old CEO husband, she replied that she had always been drawn to puissance. That tended to end conversations as people went to go look up “puissance.”

def: Physical beauty
example: Marilyn Monroe’s mystique is based not only on her obvious pulchritude, but also on her mysterious death and likely dalliance with JFK.

def: Having a sharp taste or smell; biting, stimulating, sharp

def: Cowardly, timid

def: Given to complaining, grumbling
example: Norma had been happy to be a grandmother, but was somewhat less happy when a querulous child was dropped off on her doorstep—“I don’t want to come inside,” “I don’t like sandwiches,” “It’s too cold in the bathroom.” Would the whining and moaning ever stop?

def: Quiet, still
example: After hours of moaning and shaking from his illness, the child finally exhausted himself and grew quiescent.

def: Extremely impractical but very romantic, chivalrous, or idealistic; impulsive
example: Prompted by a lesson their teacher devised for election year, the children shared what they would do if elected President. The plans were adorably quixotic, involving housing all the homeless in floating homes on the ocean, or teaching everyone to be nice to each other.

def: Witty storyteller
example: Miguel was quite the raconteur—the laughing party guests naturally congregated in a cluster around him as he held court.

def: Lofty, very high up or elevated (in a metaphorical way); exclusive, select; thin, pure, or less dense (as air at the top of a mountain)

def: Something that reacts; a substance that undergoes a change in a chemical reaction

def: Not obedient, resisting authority, hard to manage

def: Withdraw, retract, or disavow something one has previously said, esp. formally

example: I’m sorry I had to leave your presentation to take a call—I only have a minute, but can you recapitulate what you’re proposing?

def: Not easily understood, hidden, dealing with an obscure topic

def: Revival, breaking out into renewed activity
example: The recrudescence of his psoriasis came at the worst possible time. “Oh, great,” he said— now I’m going to be shedding skin flakes all over my new coworkers on the first day of work.

def: To have a good or bad effect, esp. as a result of a person’s efforts or actions (usually used with to, on, or upon)

def: Setting something right after a misdeed, compensation or relief for injury or wrongdoing (noun); correct, set right, remedy (verb)

def: Stubbornly disobedient, hard to manage
example: No matter how much job training the city gives them, refractory ex-criminals are simply unemployable.

def: Shining, radiant
example: Her new engagement ring was refulgent—she was so happy with it. I’ll bet she polished it every night.

def: Response or reply, esp. a witty comeback
example: In retrospect, I could have come up with a better rejoinder than “I know you are, but what am I?” I always think of the perfect witty comeback hours after I actually needed it.

def: Tear violently, esp. to tear one’s clothing or hair out of grief; pull apart, split, or tear away
example: Many figures in the Bible rent their clothing from grief at a loved one’s death, an event that can surely rend one’s heart as well.

def: A meal (noun); to eat or feast (verb)
example: After a light repast in a country inn, the men got back on their horses and rode away.

def: Pertaining to a repertory or repertoire, a stock of available things or a number of theatrical performances presented regularly or in sequence

def: The act or state of resting; peacefulness, tranquility; lying dead in a grave

def: Disreputable, unprincipled, or damned person (noun); shameless, depraved (adj)

def: Having a revival, renewing, rising or surging again

def: Renovate, redo, revise (verb); a restructuring, upgrade, etc. (noun)

def: Using or relating to obscene or vulgar humor

def: Dominated or burdened by

def: A gap or fissure (such as in rock), a break in friendly relations

def: Learned person, scholar, someone admitted to membership in a scholarly field; a person with amazing mental abilities despite having a cognitive difference or disability
example: The TED conferences feature savants and newsmakers speaking on topics of great importance to the world.

def: A tiny bit or trace

def: Contemptible, mean

def: In a searching or penetrating manner; while examining closely or probing for answers

def: Produce and release a substance from a cell or gland of the body for a functional purpose

def: Inciting rebellion against a government, esp. speech or writing that does this

def: Relating to the different meanings of words or other symbols
example: Bob said plastic surgery should be covered under the health care plan and Marion said it shouldn’t, but it turns out that their disagreement was purely semantic—what Bob meant was reconstructive surgery and what Marion meant was cosmetic surgery.

def: Like an angel; serene, spiritually carried off or transported
example: The gospel choir looked seraphic in their shimmering white robes.

def: Fragment of some brittle substance, esp. a sharp fragment of pottery, glass, etc.

def: A job or position that pays while requiring little or no work

def: Shy, fickle, uncertain, or prone to act suddenly due to nervousness; lively in a restless or excessive way

def: Satisfy (esp. thirst), cool, or refresh; make less active

def: A nickname
example: James Brown, often referred to with the sobriquet “The Godfather of Soul,” scored numerous smash hits and was also known for his feverish dancing.

def: Nonstandard use of grammar or words; mistake, esp. in etiquette

def: Fellowship in interests, feelings, responsibilities, etc., such as among a group of people or among classes, nations, etc.

def: Of the body

def: Disgusting, filthy, foul, extremely neglected

def: Crush, squash; suppress or silence; walk through ooze or in wet shoes, making a smacking or sucking sound
example: The repressive government squelched the rebellion immediately.

def: Immersed (in), saturated (with)

def: Very loud and powerful (generally of a human voice)

def: Mark of disgrace, a figurative stain or mark on someone’s reputation
example: In the 1950s, bearing a child out of wedlock was severely stigmatized, but today in many social circles, there is no stigma whatsoever to unmarried parents having a child.

def: Period of time spent doing something, or a specific, limited amount of work (noun); to be frugal, to get by on little (verb)

def: Lofty or elevated, inspiring reverence or awe; excellent, majestic; complete, utter

def: A court order requiring a person to appear in court and give testimony

def: Make dirty, stain, tarnish, defile

def: Person devoted to pleasure and luxury
example: The reality show about Beverly Hills “housewives” portrayed wealthy sybarites who actually seemed to be pursuing champagne and Pilates full-time.

def: Mutually dependent relationship between two organisms, people, groups, etc.

def: Relating to a synopsis or summary; giving a general view
example: The movie studio had interns read screenplays and write up synoptic outlines for the executives to review.

example: Now that my linguistics class is studying syntax, it makes a little more sense when my computer flashes “SYNTAX ERROR” at me.

def: Gaudy, cheap or cheap-looking; indecent

example: I am starting to realize that this law firm hired me to be its token woman. There I am, smiling in all the ads—but I never actually get to work on important cases.

def: Exaggerated, debased, or grotesque imitation

def: forceful or vigorous, effective, keen; caustic, sharp

def: Fierce, cruel, savage; belligerent

def: Beginner

def: Charging interest on a loan, esp. charging illegally high or excessive interest

def: Having the appearance of truth, probable

def: Through, by means of, by way of (by a route that goes through or touches)

def: Pep, enthusiasm, vitality, lively spirit

def: Extremely infectious, poisonous, etc.; hateful, bitterly hostile

def: Thick, adhesive, or covered in something sticky

def: Unnaturally pale, or showing some other indication of sickness, unhappiness, etc.; weak, lacking forcefulness

def: Withered, shriveled
